name: Glaucous-Grey
lede: Glaucous-Grey is a pale green-grey, the grey half of the same glaucous family that gives us Glaucous-Blue, standardized by Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: The grey side of glaucous
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* places Glaucous-Grey on plate XLVIII, hue 37 (five primes), tone f [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary repeats it on plate 35, swatch B2, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as a light bluish gray, block 190 [1]. Like [[glaucous-blue|Glaucous-Blue]], our data tags it as a modifier of the family word [[glaucous]] [1].

The closest common color word in our library is [[ash|Ash]], under four units away in CIEDE2000, and its nearest library neighbor is [[pale-green-blue-grey|Pale Green-Blue Grey]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Glaucous-Grey covers at least five percent of the canvas in 494 of our 23,781 paintings, 2.08 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 333 [2]. That ranks it ahead of 78 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It is most common in the Impressionist movement, twelve of 140 paintings there, 2.2 times the expected rate, and it most often plays a light, in 56 percent of its 333 appearances [2].

Philips Wouwerman is its most devoted painter, seven of his 36 paintings here, 7.5 times the rate of the museums those works come from [2]. It shares canvases with [[greenish-grey|Greenish Grey]] and [[greyish-white|Greyish White]] more than chance would predict, with lifts of 3.9 and 2.4 [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1320, 592 years before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a pigment that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
